summary: Specifies IANA registration procedures for MIME external body access types and content transfer encodings. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: MIME is how email describes its attachments. This memo says how to add new kinds of descriptions to the official list.

questions: how to register a mime transfer encoding
what is a mime external body access type
subtitle: How new MIME external body access types and transfer encodings get onto the official IANA lists.

tldr.problem: MIME is an open-ended framework, so new access types and transfer encodings keep being proposed, and the set of such values needs to be developed in an orderly, well-specified and public manner.
tldr.mechanism: Access types go through a two-week public review on a mailing list and an appointed reviewer before IANA registers them. Transfer encodings must go through the IESG and end up as standards-track RFCs.
tldr.outcome: This Best Current Practice replaces RFC 2048 and sets strict requirements, such as a public specification, a unique name and fully described security issues. Media types and charsets are handled elsewhere.

today: RFC 4289 is a Best Current Practice that obsoletes RFC 2048, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why MIME Needs Registration
sections.content:
MIME is an open-ended framework: it can accommodate additional object types, charsets and access methods without any changes to the basic protocol. A registration process is needed so that the set of such values is developed in an orderly, well-specified and public manner.

RFC 4289 defines procedures that use the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) as a central registry. It covers two kinds of value: external body access types and content transfer encodings. Registration of media types and charsets is specified in separate documents (RFC 4288 and RFC 2978) and is not addressed here.
sections.plainLanguage: If everybody made up their own labels, nobody would understand each other. So there is one official list, and this memo says how to get on it.

sections.title: Access Type Requirements
sections.content:
RFC 2046 defines the message/external-body media type, where a MIME entity acts as a pointer to the real body data instead of including it. Each reference names an access type, which determines the mechanism used to retrieve the data. New access types can be registered to cover new retrieval mechanisms.

A new access type MUST meet four requirements:

  • Naming: a unique name, used in the access-type parameter and conforming to MIME parameter syntax.
  • Mechanism: all protocols, transports and procedures must be publicly described in enough detail for any competent implementor. Secret or proprietary methods are expressly prohibited.
  • Publication: the access type MUST be described by an RFC. It may be informational, though standards-track review is encouraged.
  • Security: known security issues MUST be fully described. The access type need not be secure, but known risks must be identified.
sections.plainLanguage: A new way of fetching an attachment needs a unique name, a public instruction sheet and an honest list of dangers before it can join the list.

sections.title: How an Access Type Gets Registered
sections.content:
Registration starts with an Internet Draft. The proposal is sent to the ietf-types@iana.org mailing list for a two-week review period. Proposed access types are not formally registered and must not be used in the meantime.

After the two weeks, the access type reviewer, appointed by the IETF Applications Area Director(s), either forwards the request to iana@iana.org or rejects it because of significant objections raised on the list. The decision must be posted to the list within 14 days, and it may be appealed to the IESG as specified in RFC 2026.

IANA registers the access type once it has passed review or won an appeal. The specification must also be published as an RFC. IANA learns who the reviewer is from the IESG, and acts only on requests the reviewer forwards or on an IESG notice that an appeal overturned the reviewer.
sections.plainLanguage: You post your idea for two weeks so people can comment. Then a referee says yes or no, and if you disagree you can ask a higher board.

sections.title: Transfer Encodings
sections.content:
Transfer encodings are transformations applied to MIME media types after conversion to canonical form. The RFC lists three purposes: turning binary data into text that survives transports limited to short lines or a small subset of US-ASCII (such as base64 and quoted-printable from RFC 2045), compressing large entities with general-purpose non-lossy compression, and representing existing encoding formats in a MIME context.

The RFC says plainly that standardizing many different transfer encodings is a significant barrier to widespread interoperability and is expressly discouraged. The procedure exists only for the case where standardization is really justified.
sections.plainLanguage: Some mail systems can only carry plain text, so attachments get wrapped in a text disguise. This memo says new disguises are strongly discouraged.

sections.title: Transfer Encoding Requirements
sections.content:
A new transfer encoding MUST meet these requirements:

  • Name: unique, and conforming to the syntax of the Content-Transfer-Encoding header field.
  • Algorithms: described in their entirety. Secret or proprietary algorithms are expressly prohibited in standardized transfer encodings.
  • Input: applicable to an arbitrary sequence of octets of any length. The 7bit and 8bit encodings do not meet this, and the rule forbids adding encodings similar to or redundant with them.
  • Output: fully documented, including whether it always stays within 7bit or 8bit or is pure binary.
  • Invertible: the original data must be recoverable on any platform. This excludes lossy compression and all forms of encryption.
  • New functionality: some overlap is fine, but it MUST offer something no other transfer encoding provides.
  • Security: SHOULD NOT contain known security issues, and any known issues MUST be fully described.
sections.plainLanguage: A new disguise must work on any file, be fully reversible, and do something the old ones cannot. Scrambling a secret on purpose does not count.

sections.title: The Transfer Encoding Process
sections.content:
Definition starts with an Internet Draft that defines the encoding precisely and gives substantial justification for standardizing it. It is presented to the IESG, which can reject it outright, assign it to an existing working group, approve a new working group, or accept it as-is for processing as an individual standards-track submission.

An encoding is considered defined and available for use once it is on the standards track. No special IANA procedure is needed: all legitimate registrations MUST appear as standards-track RFCs, so the IESG notifies IANA when one is approved. The lists live at the IANA access-types and transfer-encodings pages.
sections.plainLanguage: For a new disguise, a big committee decides whether the idea is worth it. If yes, it goes through the normal standards process.
